activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: After the 1929 crash, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932.
story:
Sofia dragged the folding table out of the garage at eight in the morning, before the sun had fully cleared the rooftops. Her lemonade stand was not really about lemonade anymore. It was about the twenty dollars she had promised to add to Grandpa's birthday present, a frame for the old photograph of his father holding a bank book from 1929. For her history project she had found a record showing that after the 1929 crash, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932. Her great-grandfather had put his savings into stocks right before that, and the money had never come back. She kept thinking about the number as she squeezed lemons: 89 percent, gone.

Ali arrived on a bike with a dented basket, skidding to a stop in the gravel. "You said you needed help. Is this about the project, or the money?"

"Both. I have to explain which is riskier, a stock or a bond, and why, and I keep getting tangled." Sofia poured a cup for the mail carrier, who waved and kept walking. "Ms. Clarke-Williams said to imagine explaining it to somebody at a lemonade stand. So I thought, actual lemonade stand."

Ryker showed up at ten with a notebook full of practice problems, because Ryker showed up to everything with a notebook. "Okay, test me," he said, holding out a cup. "Stocks and bonds. Bonds first."

"Ms. Clarke-Williams says bonds are like lending the stand ten dollars and it pays you back with a little extra," Sofia said. "Stocks are like owning a piece of the stand itself."

"Then stocks seem better," Ali said. "If the stand does great, your piece is worth more."

"Unless the whole town decides nobody wants lemonade ever again," Sofia said slowly. An idea was forming, and she reached for a marker and the cardboard sign. "Wait. I can test this."

She wrote two columns on the sign's blank side and labeled them with her neatest printing. Then she asked Ali to be the bond. "You lent the stand five dollars. Whatever happens, you get five dollars and a quarter back. Ryker, you own a tenth of the stand." She counted the morning's cash: eleven dollars and some coins. "Ryker gets a tenth of everything, good day or bad."

They played it out three times with imaginary days, a busy Saturday, a rainy Tuesday, a heat wave. Ali's nickel never changed. Ryker's take swung wildly, sometimes a pile of quarters, sometimes almost nothing. "So you can't just categorize one as good and one as bad," Sofia said, drawing an arrow between the columns. "The bond is a promise. The stock is a bet on the stand itself."

"The prototype of risk," Ryker said, pointing at the stock column.

Ali frowned at the sign. "But how bad can a real bet get?"

Sofia told them the number, the whole thing, the crash and the peak and the low. Ali was quiet for a moment, staring at the photograph sticking out of Sofia's binder, the bank book and the face above it. "Eighty-nine percent," Ali said. "That's like the stand burning down and taking Ryker's tenth with it, and then the lot going empty for three years."

"And the bond holder still gets paid back," Ryker said, "if whoever borrowed doesn't vanish."

"Unless," Sofia said, and wrote that word on the sign too, smaller, in the corner.

Ms. Clarke-Williams stopped by on her walk that afternoon and bought two cups. She read the cardboard sign, both columns, the arrows, the small word in the corner. "This is a market," she said, indicating the table, the cups, the line of neighborhood kids.

Sofia counted out Ryker's tenth of the day's earnings, four quarters and a dime, and dropped them into his palm. "Owing beats owning," he said, and Ali held up her fixed nickel like a trophy.

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: Mandarin Chinese verbs do not change form for tense; a future plan is shown with time words like "míngnián" (next year) or helper words like "huì" (will).
story:
Elizabeth slid the Mandarin grammar book across the library table so fast it thumped into Francis's elbow. "Help," she said. "The paragraph is due Friday, and I can't find the future tense anywhere."

Francis rubbed his elbow and pulled the book toward his stack of notes. "It has to be in here," he said. "Spanish had a whole chapter on it. I need the same one, because my paragraph is about joining the robotics club next year, and Ms. Menon said it has to be about our real plans."

They flipped pages together while the radiators ticked and rain streaked the tall windows. Elizabeth found chapters on measure words and tone marks, but no chart of future endings. She sat back, frustrated. "Maybe the book is missing pages," she said. "Maybe someone tore them out."

"Nobody tore out a grammar chart," Francis said. He was already checking the index, which was its own kind of help, because it gave Elizabeth an idea.

"If the pages aren't missing," she said slowly, "maybe there's nothing to find. Maybe the verbs don't change at all." She grabbed a pencil and wrote the sentence she remembered from Monday's reading, the one about pandas being nocturnal, since their insulation of thick fur kept them warm even at night. Then she wrote her own sentence: next year she would join the art club. She looked at the two sentences side by side. The verb looked exactly the same in both. Same characters, same shape.

She found the difference somewhere else. The panda sentence had no time word. Her sentence had "míngnián," which meant next year, right at the front, doing all the work. She tested it, saying both sentences out loud under her breath while Francis watched. "The time word carries it," she said. "The whole future rides on that."

"So there's no future ending," Francis said, "because the verb never changes?"

"Right. And look." She pointed at a second word in her notes, "huì," sitting before the verb in a dialogue example. "This one helps too. It means will." Francis copied both words onto his palm with his marker, since he kept losing his index card, and wrote his robotics sentence with "míngnián" at the start.

They worked until the librarian flicked the lights once, her signal that the library closed in ten minutes. Elizabeth packed her bag, then saw Francis still frowning at his paragraph. She pulled out her grammar book and slid it across the table to him.

"Take it home," she said. "I've got what I need. Page forty-one, the panda part, in case you forget."

Francis grinned and zipped the book into his backpack just as the lights went dark. "Next year," he said, "huì," and held the door for her.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Naomi sat in the lobby of Castlefall, refreshing the clan list for the third time, because the Emberhawks had one open slot and tryouts closed at nine. Her headset crackled.

"You're the girl from the picture, right?" said a player whose tag was VexNine. "Karlee's friend. The one at the lake, blue kayak?"

Naomi's hand froze on the mouse. She had never seen VexNine before in her life. "How do you know about the kayak?"

"Someone posted it. Public clan album, like two years ago. It's got your whole names in the caption. Naomi plus last name."

She dropped out of the queue and opened a search engine in another window. She typed her own full name, half expecting nothing. The fifth result was a comment she had written in fifth grade on the Castlefall forums, calling a character named Lord Bramble the best antagonist ever written and signing it with her real name and her town. Below it, a link to the kayak photo, captioned by Karlee: "Naomi and me at Pine Lake!" The lake name was right there. Anyone who read it knew where she swam in summer.

Ronald joined the party channel. "You dropped queue. Tryout's in ten."

"Someone found a photo of me. From a public post Karlee made." She kept scrolling, systematic about it now, checking each result, working out which posts had her name and which didn't. The pattern was simple: the public stuff showed up, the private clan chat didn't. She ran a test, typing a phrase from an old private message into the search bar. Nothing came back. She typed a phrase from the public forum comment. First result.

"It's crawlers," VexNine said. "Automated programs that copy public pages so search engines can index them."

"So anything public gets copied," Naomi said slowly. "And it stays findable."

She messaged Karlee, who was offline, then went into her own old account and deleted the forum comment, all forty-one of them, one by one. The kayak photo she couldn't touch; it was Karlee's post. She rejoined the queue with four minutes left, won her duel, and got the Emberhawk slot.

Afterward she celebrated with Ronald in voice chat, though it felt thinner than she'd imagined. Then a clan notification popped up. The Emberhawks' roster page was public, and her full gamertag, which contained her real first name, had just been published to it. She watched the page load, knowing that somewhere a crawler was already on its way.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Gavin spread his boxes across the driveway at seven in the morning: old comics, a bin of plastic dinosaurs, three board games with all their pieces counted twice. His goal was fifty dollars for the robotics kit he'd seen online, and by eight he had made four. The problem, he decided, was not what he was selling. It was the price.

His neighbour Mr. Singh ran the garage sale next door, and Mr. Singh had the crowd. He had a crate of glass marbles, nothing special, and he had taped a sign to it that said TWENTY-FIVE CENTS EACH. A line of kids stretched past the mailbox. Gavin watched a boy buy eight marbles, come back ten minutes later, and buy six more.

"Those are just marbles," Gavin said to his friend Kane, who had shown up to help and was eating chips on the porch steps. "My dinosaurs are better."

"Then charge more for the dinosaurs," Kane said. Kane wanted a cut of the profits, ten percent, because he had carried the boxes from the basement and planned to stand at the curb shouting at cars all morning. Gavin told him he could have five percent if the shouting worked.

The shouting did not work. At a dollar per dinosaur, nobody touched them. At three for a dollar, a woman with a stroller bought six, but that was it. Gavin sat on the steps and tried to think it through the way his math teacher talked about quantifying things, putting actual numbers to a guess instead of just feeling that something was true. Fewer buyers at a higher price. More buyers at a lower one. The same box of dinosaurs both times, the same driveway, the same sky. Only the number on the sign had changed.

He looked over at Mr. Singh's table again. The marble line was gone, and Mr. Singh was reading a newspaper with his feet up. Gavin walked over. "What happened to your customers?"

"Sold the crate," Mr. Singh said. "A man came by and offered to take every marble I had. Volume business. When I first opened, though, I charged a dime each, and I could barely keep the jar full. Kids were back three times in an hour." He folded the newspaper. "Law of demand," he said, and went back to reading.

Gavin went back to his driveway and made a new sign. DINOSAURS, TEN CENTS. By ten o'clock the bin was nearly empty, and Jillian from his science class was arguing that the triceratops should cost more than the others because it was the only one with all three horns intact. Kane stood at the curb yelling "Aggressive deals, prehistoric prices!" at every passing car, which Gavin decided was worth the five percent. When the last dinosaur sold, Jillian held out a dime for the triceratops, and Gavin slid it across the table to her for free, because she'd been right, and because a kid who knew a bargain was worth keeping around.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, all lines going straight back into the distance meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.
story:
Audrey pressed her sketchbook against the railing on the gallery's mezzanine and stared down at the big photograph on the far wall. It showed an empty street running straight back between two rows of buildings, and it was exactly the kind of picture she wanted to draw for the summer art contest. The theme was "My Street," and the deadline was Sunday, which gave her three days.

Her problem was simple and enormous: her streets looked wrong. Last night she had drawn the road outside her house four times, and every time it came out like a wedge of pie floating in the middle of the page. She had shown the drawings to her dad, who said they were nice, but nice was not the same as right.

"Audrey! Over here!" Ayana waved from the other end of the mezzanine, with Hendrik beside her holding a lemonade. The three of them had walked to the gallery after Ms. Nguyen had given them free passes from the community center.

"Look at this photo," Audrey said as they reached her. "The street looks like it goes back for miles, but it's flat paper. Flat paper with lines on it."

Hendrik leaned over the railing. "The buildings on the sides aren't smaller in real life."

"Right!" Audrey flipped her sketchbook to her failed drawings. "And my road edges are doing this." She traced them with her pencil. Both edges slanted inward, but they were aimed at different spots, and her sidewalk lines wandered off toward a third. Three different directions, none of them meeting anywhere.

Ayana squinted at the photo, then at Audrey's page, then at the photo again. "In the picture, the road edges come together. Like, actually together. Somewhere near that far door."

Audrey grabbed a fresh page. "One point. What if all of them, every line going back, they all have to hit the same point?" She held her pencil at arm's length toward the photograph, lining it up with the left road edge, then the right, then the sidewalk lines, then the rooflines of the buildings. The pencil kept landing on the same tiny patch of gray near the horizon, right where a distant door glowed in the street's far end. She felt a revolution start in her chest, like someone had flipped a drawing inside out.

"Here," she said, and drew a horizontal line across her page, then a single dot on it. "Vanishing point." She said the word out loud and it felt like a key turning. "And the line it sits on, that's where the horizon is. It's eye level. If I'm standing on the street looking straight ahead, that's where it goes."

She drew fast now. Road edges from the bottom corners straight to the dot. Sidewalk lines to the dot. Building edges to the dot. Then she drew the verticals, the fronts of buildings, standing straight up and down, and the whole street dropped into place on the page like it had been waiting there the whole time. She could not stop grinning.

"That's it," Hendrik said. "That's actually it."

"Ms. Nguyen said the gallery closes in ten minutes," Ayana said, tugging her sleeve.

"Ten minutes is three buildings." Audrey was already ruling the next line toward the dot, her pencil rushing to keep up with the street appearing under it.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Teen safety guides advise telling a parent or trusted adult where you are going, who you will be with and when you will be home.
story:
William had fifteen dollars in his pocket and one text left to send before his phone died. He stood near the ticket booth at the football field, watching for Priya's blue jacket, and typed fast: "Going to the game with Priya and Arthur and Titan. Home by nine." His mom answered with a thumbs-up before he could even worry about it.

The plan had started in science class, of all places. Titan had leaned over during a worksheet and said, "My sister texts my mom everything before she leaves. Where she's going, who she's with, when she'll be home. Every single time, like a reflex." William had filed that away, and this morning he had tested it by asking his mom, casually, what she'd want to know if he went somewhere Friday night. She listed the same three things without hesitating. That settled it. Three facts, sent in advance, and nobody could say he hadn't been careful.

Priya arrived at the gate with Arthur trailing behind her, carrying a bag of popcorn he had clearly already started. They paid and pushed through the turnstile into the noise of the crowd. The bleachers were packed, so they migrated toward the empty seats at the far end, near the fence, where the sound of the game reached them a beat late. William bought two hot chocolates, since Priya's hands were cold, and managed not to drop either one.

In the third quarter his phone buzzed with a low battery warning, and then it died for good. He felt a small twist of panic, then reminded himself that the whole point of the earlier text was that the plan already existed somewhere outside his phone. His mom knew where he was. She knew who he was with. She knew nine o'clock. He didn't need to explain anything to anyone.

At two minutes to nine, they walked to the parking lot together. Priya's older brother was already idling at the curb. "Text me when you're home," she said, and Arthur made a face like he might be sick, and Titan laughed so loudly that a man walking past looked over.

William's mom was in the driveway when the brother's car pulled up. She was holding her car keys, not her phone, and the porch light was on. "You made it with two minutes to spare," she said. Then, quieter, "Thanks for the text. That's how I knew exactly where to come if I'd needed to." A strand of Stadium lights still glowed orange behind the trees at the end of the street.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
The community centre homework club met in the room behind the gym, where the windows looked out on a lush wall of ivy that nobody ever trimmed. Evelyn spread her worksheet on the long table and read the first problem again: 2x + 3x = 25. She wanted a spot on the school math team, and Ms. Asante had told her that today's practice sheet was the tryout, collected at four o'clock sharp.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," said Peyton, sliding into the next chair.

"Feel like it." Evelyn tapped her pencil on the paper. She knew the rule was to do the same thing to both sides, but 2x + 3x had two pieces on the left and she didn't know what to do with them first.

Across the table, Emilien wrote something fast and confident. Evelyn leaned over, hoping for a hint, and her stomach dropped. He had written 5x = 25.

"How did you get that?" she asked.

"Easy. Two plus three is five."

Before she could answer, Ms. Asante passed behind them and set a battered binder on the table. "Loaner binder," she said. "Pages in the back are loose. Mind the envelope, it's not mine." She moved on to the far table, and Evelyn forgot about the envelope because Emilien was already copying his answer onto the tryout sheet.

She couldn't let him turn that in. If he did, the whole room would ridicule him when it came back marked wrong, and she knew how that felt. But she didn't know why it was wrong, only that something about it itched. Two x's and a plain three. She thought of the ivy outside: vines and bricks. You could add vines to vines, but bricks were something else.

She opened the binder to hunt for a similar problem. The loose pages crackled and the envelope slipped out, sealed, with her name on it. Her actual name, Evelyn, in handwriting she almost recognized. She tore it open.

Dear whoever gets this binder, the note began. I failed the tryout last year because of one thing, so I'm writing it down for you. 2x + 3x becomes 5x. Like terms combine. But 2x and 3 cannot be combined, because one has a variable and one does not. There is no x to add to the 3. It was signed with only a smiley face, and Evelyn sat very still, because Emilien had just done the exact thing the letter warned about.

"Emilien," she said, keeping her voice low, "what does your x stand for?"

He looked at his page. "Something I don't know yet, I guess."

"So you're adding three of something you don't know to two of something you don't know. Then tell me what the 3 is three of."

He stared at his pencil. Peyton pulled the letter across the table, read it twice, and said, "Who wrote this?"

Evelyn turned the envelope over. On the back, in the same handwriting, was a single line: I got the next one right.

She slid the letter to Emilien, picked up her own pencil, and wrote 5x = 25 on the first problem, where both terms had x's. Outside, a breeze moved through the ivy, every leaf shifting at once.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In French, "Je voudrais..." means "I would like..." and sounds more polite than "Je veux...", which means "I want..."
story:
Ava stood at Kaia's kitchen counter, which Kaia had declared "the restaurant," and tried to remember the word for water. It was Friday, and on Tuesday their French class would take a bus to a real crêpe place across town, where they had to order entirely in French. Ava's grade depended on it, and so did her pride, because she had told Colin she would order for both of them.

"Bonjour," said Kaia, holding a notebook like a waiter's pad. "Que voulez-vous?" She had stacked the counter with cereal boxes and a plate of toast, and their friend Colin sat at the table as the only other customer, drumming his fork against his glass.

"Je veux une crêpe," Ava said, proud of herself. She had practiced that sentence all week.

Kaia put her hands on her hips. "Excuse me?" she said, in English, stepping out of her waiter role. She looked genuinely annoyed, which surprised Ava, because Kaia never got annoyed at anything.

"What did I say?" Ava asked. Colin stopped drumming.

"That was so rude," Kaia said. "You basically barked at me." She flipped her notebook open to a page where she had copied sentences from their textbook. "Try again."

Ava frowned. She replayed the moment in her head. She hadn't shouted, and her pronunciation had been fine, she was almost sure of it. So what had changed the room? It had to be the verb. She thought about English for a second: nobody at a real restaurant said "I want water." They said "I would like." Maybe French worked the same way. She tested the idea the only way she could.

"Je voudrais une crêpe," she said, slower this time.

Kaia's whole face changed. "Perfect!" she said. "See, 'Je voudrais' means 'I would like.' 'Je veux' just means 'I want.' Big difference." She turned back to her pad. "C'est combien?" she added, tapping the cereal box as if it had a price.

"Um," said Ava, and her mind went blank. "Combien... ça coûte?" It came out as a question, but Kaia nodded so hard her braids bounced, and Colin clapped once, which made him knock his glass over. It rolled off the table and landed on the rug without breaking.

"My neurons are fried," Colin announced, rubbing his temples, "but you've got it. Say the whole thing to me. I'm the waiter now."

"Je voudrais une crêpe au chocolat," Ava said to Colin, standing straighter. "C'est combien?"

"Cinq euros," Colin said, in the worst accent Ava had ever heard, holding up five fingers arranged in a line almost perpendicular to his palm, like a tiny fence.

On Tuesday, when the real waiter came to their table, Ava heard her own voice come out steady. "Je voudrais une crêpe au fromage, s'il vous plaît." The waiter smiled and wrote it down. Across the table, Colin raised his water glass and mouthed, "C'est combien?"

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
story:
Cameron stood at the white line of the school track, the morning sun warming the rubber under his shoes and the smell of cut grass drifting from the football field. Mr. Diallo clicked his stopwatch and held it up.

"Eight hundred metres, two laps. Go when you're ready."

Last Saturday's race still stung in Cameron's mind. He had blasted off the line like a rocket, arms pumping, and led the whole first lap while the crowd shouted his name. Then his legs turned to concrete on the back straight of lap two, and three runners streamed past him before the finish. Damian had won, and afterward, in the changeroom, Damian and Davis compared lap times.

"First lap sixty-two, second lap seventy-one," Damian said, reading from his phone.

Davis whistled. "Mine was the other way around. Sixty-eight, then sixty-four. My second lap was faster than my first."

"That's a negative split," Damian said. "Running the second half faster. Mine was a positive split, faster first half."

Cameron had stared at the floor, because his own splits were the worst of all. Sixty, then seventy-eight. His legs hadn't just faded, they had collapsed, and there had to be a reason he couldn't see. It wasn't that he lacked speed. Something hidden was eating it. He turned the two sets of numbers over all week and formed an idea: if the fastest first lap made the slowest second lap, maybe the trick was to hold something back on purpose, like saving the best slice of pizza for last.

Now he raised his hand before the start. "I'm going to try running the first lap slower on purpose."

Davis, leaning on the railing with a water bottle, groaned. "I need you to pace me for my time trial next week. If you jog the first lap, that ruins my pacing." Davis had his own plan: he wanted a negative split so big that Mr. Diallo would pick him for the city relay team, and he needed a rabbit, someone to chase.

"Fine," Cameron said. "Chase me anyway. I'll be just ahead."

Mr. Diallo's whistle cracked the air. Cameron went out controlled, legs light, lungs easy, holding a rhythm that felt almost too comfortable. Davis hammered past him at the bend, exactly as planned, and Cameron let him go, counting his own effort like coins in a pocket. He crossed the first lap right behind Davis's shoulder.

Then the test. Cameron lifted his knees, drove his arms, and found, to his amazement, a whole tank of fuel still waiting. He surged past Davis on the final curve, spikes gripping, the wind cold on his teeth, and sprinted the home straight so hard his vision narrowed to the finish line.

Mr. Diallo called out the splits. "Sixty-nine, then sixty-three. Second lap faster than your first. Negative split, Cameron."

Cameron bent over, laughing between breaths. "It works!"

Davis jogged up, grinning. "Do that at my trial. Stay one metre ahead of me the whole way."

"Deal," Cameron said, and shook on it, sweat cooling on his neck.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Avery stood in Cloe's bedroom while Cloe dumped a shoebox of glow stick bracelets onto the bed. The dance started in an hour, and the theme was Glow Night, which meant everyone would be walking around like fireflies.

"My mom bought these because she's frugal," Cloe said, sorting the stiff plastic tubes into piles. "Ones already cracked are half price, but half of them don't work."

Avery picked one up. It was dark, just a pale tube. She bent it anyway, and nothing happened. A second one, nothing. The third gave a faint green flicker and died.

"They're not broken batteries," Avery said slowly. "Something inside has to mix. When you bend it, you must be breaking something." She held a dead one up to Cloe's lamp, squinting. "I can't see a seam or a vial or anything. But every one that works, works after a hard snap. Every one that doesn't, doesn't."

"So snap harder," Cloe said.

Avery pressed the dead tube against the edge of the bed frame and pushed until she felt a tiny click, like a seed cracking. Green light spilled across the comforter.

"Told you," Cloe said.

At the dance, the gym was so dark the bleachers looked like they'd vanished. Israel appeared beside them with a bracelet glowing orange on his wrist. "Where's the light even coming from?" he said, turning it over. "There's no bulb. I checked."

"You crack a little glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside," Avery said. "It mixes with other chemicals and a dye, and the reaction makes light. It's called chemiluminescence."

Israel stared at her. "How do you know that?"

"She tested it," Cloe said. "On my bed frame. With science."

Halfway through the night the principal walked the floor with a clipboard, and Avery watched him stop a group of eighth graders near the door. One of them was shaking a glow stick like a maraca, flinging drops. The liquid speckled the gym floor in little orange dots.

"That's a citation," Israel whispered. "He's getting a citation."

Avery laughed, then caught herself. A splatter of orange had landed near her shoe. She wiped it carefully with her sleeve and held her own bracelet up high, where its glow washed green across her knuckles. "Come on," she said, and pulled Cloe toward the music.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
Isla spread her homework across the kitchen table: a worksheet, her history textbook, and a shoebox her grandmother had mailed from the attic. The assignment said, "Use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." Isla underlined primary twice. What did that even mean?

Inside the shoebox, wrapped in a dish towel, was a thin booklet with a cracked leather cover. Her grandmother's note said it was a copy of a diary kept by one of their ancestors, a woman named Ruth who had walked part of the trail west when she was sixteen. Isla turned the brittle-feeling pages, which were actually reprinted paper, and read the first line out loud. "We left because the land was tired and Papa said Ohio would let us thrive." She frowned. Thrive. The land was tired? How could land be tired?

She reached for the textbook instead, because textbooks had answers. She found a chapter with a tidy paragraph about people moving west for farmland, opportunity and railroads. It was clear and organized, and she copied two sentences before stopping. Something felt off. Why did Ruth say the land was tired, and the textbook say nothing about tired land?

A memory surfaced from last month, the field trip to the history museum. Their guide, Mr. Gill, had held up an old letter behind glass. "This is called a primary source," he had said, "something made at the time by a person who lived through an event." Then he'd pointed at a poster on the wall. "That poster is a secondary source, written later by someone studying it." Isla had been half listening, wondering if the letter smelled like old paper, but now the words came back sharp and clear.

She looked at the diary, then at the textbook, then at the diary again. Ruth wrote her words while walking west, while living it. The textbook was written a hundred years later by somebody who studied it. So the diary was the primary source, and the textbook wasn't. That meant the assignment wasn't asking for the neat summary. It was asking for Ruth.

Isla texted her friend Tiffany: is the textbook a primary source?? Tiffany wrote back, duh, it's the main book. Isla stared at the message, then typed: no, it's a secondary source because it was written later. Ruth's diary is my primary source. She made it, and she lived it. Tiffany replied with a single word: oh.

Isla started a fresh page. She copied Ruth's line about the tired land, then flipped ahead. In one August entry, Ruth wrote that rain finally came down like a monsoon after weeks of dust, and that the oxen drank until they shook. Random details, Isla thought, but not really random. Tired land, dust, no rain, then rain. Ruth's family wasn't chasing some big idea. They were hungry for good ground. That was a reason, hiding under the dust of the page, and Isla had dug it out.

She wrote her paragraph, quoting Ruth twice. Then she propped the diary against the salt shaker so the cover faced her while she worked.

"You're the primary source," she told it.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Colton crouched on the back porch steps, holding his sketchbook at arm's length and squinting at it. The assignment was due Monday: draw the old oak tree in the yard, and he had promised Ms. Mori it would be his best work. But the tree on the page looked like a ghost, all pale gray scratchings, none of the deep shadow in the knots and under the branches.

He thought about last spring, when he'd given up on a portrait of his grandmother because it came out "washed out," as his dad said. He'd blamed the paper, blamed the light, blamed himself, and shoved the sketchbook in a drawer for weeks. He didn't want that to happen again, so this time he decided to actually figure out what had gone wrong.

"Whatcha doing?" Aleksandar called, dropping his bike on the grass and coming over. He peered at the page. "That's the tree? It looks kind of faint."

"I know." Colton turned the pencil in his fingers and read the letters stamped on the barrel. He had grabbed it from the coffee can of pencils without looking, the way he always did. It said 4H. Then he dug through the can and found another one, a 6B, and a memory surfaced: Karen, of all people, leaning over his desk in art class saying, "On drawing pencils, H is hardness and B is blackness." He'd ignored her because he'd been in a bad mood that day, and now he felt his ears go warm.

He had a theory. Maybe the faint tree wasn't his fault as an artist; maybe the tool itself was the hidden cause. He tested it by hatching a small patch of shade with the 4H, then a patch with the 6B right beside it. The 6B patch came out dark and velvety, almost like charcoal, while the 4H stayed stubbornly pale even when he pressed hard.

"So the 6B is the black one," Aleksandar said, watching. "H for hardness, B for blackness. Huh."

"Blackness," Colton repeated, and grinned. He started over on a fresh page, blocking in the trunk with the 6B, letting the soft graphite drag thick and dark across the paper. The smell of cut grass drifted over from the neighbor's mower, and a squirrel scolded them from the oak's lowest branch, almost as if it approved.

Later Karen stopped by to return a lacrosse stick, and they showed her the finished drawing, the two of them voting his new tree better than his old portrait. It was unanimous, two to one, once Karen added her hand. She laughed and said he should have listened to her months ago, and Colton couldn't argue. He thought about all the drawings sitting faint and half-finished in his drawer, drawings a different pencil might have provoked into something better. He tapped the 6B against his knee and said, "Come on, I want to show you something in the garage."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and later leans away.
story:
Declan's bedroom smelled of pencil shavings and cold pizza, and on his desk sat the worst science grade he'd ever gotten: a red C-minus on the seasons quiz. Mr. Rosen had written one comment at the top. "You told me what happens. Not why." Tomorrow he'd let students retry the question out loud, and Declan wanted that chance badly, because his father, who worked on engines all day and called pistons the honest part of any machine, had said over dinner, "Anybody can memorize. Understand it, and nobody can take it from you."

Isha came over after school carrying her dad's camping lantern and a beach-ball globe from the dollar store, the kind so cheap the countries were already obsolete, their borders printed crooked. She plunked the lamp in the middle of the room. "You're the Earth. Walk around it and show me winter."

Declan held the tilted globe and started his orbit, taking slow steps around the lantern, and it began to irritate him almost immediately, because every time he rounded the lamp he turned the globe so it always faced the light the same way, spinning it in his hands like a steering wheel. "There," he said. "Now the top half gets less sun."

"That's summer," Isha said. "You just made the top lean toward the lamp."

He stopped. He walked it again, and this time he forced himself to keep the globe's axis pointing at the same spot on the wall, at the closet door, no matter where he was in his circle. When he stood on one side of the lamp, the top half of the globe leaned toward the light, bright across all its crooked countries. When he shuffled around to the far side, still aiming the axis at the closet, the top half leaned away and the light struck it thin and slanted, like late afternoon in December. "It's not pointing at the Sun," he said slowly. "It's pointing at the same direction in space the whole year. The whole orbit. That's why the seasons flip." He grabbed a marker and drew a lopsided circle on a pizza box, an arrow poking off the globe, straight and unchanging.

The next day Mr. Rosen called on him, and Declan walked a chalk eraser around the desk lamp, axis aimed stubbornly at the window, and Mr. Rosen nodded and said, "That's the explanation. B plus." Two points short of the A, because the quiz still counted, but standing at his seat with chalk dust on his sleeve, Declan drew the crooked circle in his notebook anyway, and beside it he wrote, for his father, "nobody can take it from you."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Baking soda dissolved in water makes a mildly basic solution, with a pH of about 8 to 9.
story:
The chemistry lab on the second floor of the science museum smelled faintly of vinegar, and Cole liked it immediately. Mr. Ferreira had set out six cups of liquid, a stack of blue and pink strips, and a chart with numbers from zero to fourteen. "pH scale," he said. "Test each cup, write your result, and don't guess. The paper does the guessing." Dahlia, beside Cole, was less interested in the paper than in the prize table across the room, where the day's best lab sheet won a glow-in-the-dark mug. She had already measured her handwriting smaller so her sheet would look neat.

They worked through the cups quickly. Vinegar turned the blue paper pink, so it was an acid. Soapy water turned the pink paper blue, a base. Plain water left both strips unchanged, neutral, right in the middle at seven. Cole began to feel confident, the way you do when a pattern holds. Then Dahlia slid the last cup toward him. "Baking soda water," she said. "Bet you five points off my sheet it's neutral, same as plain water. It's mostly water anyway."

Cole dipped a blue strip. It stayed blue, which felt like half a win for her. He was about to write "neutral" when he remembered the other test. He dipped the pink strip, and it turned blue, slow and unmistakable, like sunrise deciding to happen. He held it up to the chart. "It's not neutral. Look, it's basic. Mildly basic, somewhere around eight or nine." Dahlia frowned at her cup as if it had lied to her personally. "It's an illusion," she said. "It looks exactly like water." Cole grinned. "Water with a secret."

Dahlia refused to give up on her mug so easily. She made Cole test three more strips from the same cup, watching each pink strip turn blue like the first one, and made him initial each result as a witness. When Mr. Ferreira strolled past, she flagged him down and pointed at her sheet. He checked the numbers, nodded, and slid the glow-in-the-dark mug across the table. Dahlia held it up to the light like a trophy. "See? Persevere," she said. "You were pessimistic about my five points."

"I was right about the baking soda," Cole said. "That's worth something."

"Fine." She poured him a little of the solution into a paper cup and handed him one last strip. "Prove it again."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
At 7:04 on Tuesday night, Cameron's phone buzzed so many times it nearly slid off his desk. The group chat, which was supposed to be for planning the sixth-grade carnival booth, had turned into an argument. "The booth is obviously a space station," Haider wrote. "I was in the gym after school. There's cardboard covered in foil everywhere." Leif shot back within seconds: "A space station? It's clearly a jungle. The poster by the front door has vines and a monkey on it." Cameron frowned at the screen. He had carried boxes into the storage room himself, and every single box was labeled with one word: ocean.

He typed, "I think you're both wrong," and then deleted it, because being the third person to shout into a group chat never seemed to fix anything. Instead he asked a question, the kind his mom called his wondering voice: "How can we each be so sure when we saw different things?" Haider answered with a shrugging emoji. Leif wrote, "Because I'm right." Cameron set the phone down and stared at the ceiling. Something was going on here, some hidden pattern, and it felt almost like an equation where every person had plugged in a different number and somehow all of them equaled certainty.

The next morning he asked the librarian for books about arguments, which got him a strange look but also a shelf of them. In a tattered collection of stories from ancient India he found one about blind men and an elephant. Each man touches a different part, the trunk, a leg, an ear, and each describes the animal completely differently, and each is completely sure. Cameron read it twice. Was that what had happened to the booth? Had Haider touched the foil, Leif the poster, and him the boxes, each of them holding only one piece of the whole thing?

He had a simple idea for testing it, and it only required three photos. In the chat that evening he wrote, "Do an experiment with me. Post one picture of the booth part you saw. No words, just the picture." Haider sent the foil walls. Leif sent the vine poster. Cameron sent the ocean boxes. Then he added his third photo, the one he had taken at lunch from the stage stairs, looking down at the whole gym at once. The booth was a spaceship that had crash-landed in a jungle and sunk into the sea.

The chat went quiet for almost a full minute, which in group-chat time felt like an hour. Then Leif wrote, "Oh. It's a shipwreck." Haider wrote, "I found the parable of the blind men and the elephant last night, and it's literally us." Cameron laughed out loud, alone in his room, and watched the argument dissolve into a flood of new messages about jungle vines made from green streamers and foil waves.

On carnival day, Mr. Shapiro ducked under the paper palm trees and studied the shipwreck booth for a long moment. "So which one of you dreamed this up?" he asked. Cameron pointed at Haider, and Haider pointed at Leif, and Leif pointed at Cameron.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A traditional corded phone on a copper landline usually keeps working in a power cut, because the phone company powers the line, but cordless phones need household electricity.
story:
The lights went out just as Georgia was finishing her history notes at the farmhouse kitchen table, and the whole house went dark except for the last grey light of the evening at the windows. "Mom!" she called, hearing footsteps and a bump in the hall. "Power cut," her mom said from the doorway, holding her phone up so its screen glowed. "I'll find the candles. Can you call Mariam? She's coming tomorrow and we need to tell her about the road work."

Georgia picked up the cordless phone from its cradle and pressed the button, but the screen stayed black. She pressed it again, jiggled it, held it up to the light. Dead. Of course, she thought, it plugs into the wall to charge, and it sits in a base that hums when the power is on. No power, no phone. She felt a flicker of panic. The storm had been rolling in all afternoon, and out here at the farmhouse the nearest neighbour was a field away.

Then she remembered the odd beige box on the kitchen wall, down low, near the door to the porch. Grandpa had called it the old phone. It had a curly cord and a heavy handset and a round thing you spun with your finger, and Mom had once wanted to take it down. Georgia crossed the dark kitchen, feeling her way along the counter past the plumbing under the sink, which had a chronic drip that puddled the floor no matter what. She lifted the handset and held it to her ear.

A dial tone hummed, loud and steady. Georgia almost laughed out loud. The cordless phone upstairs needed the house's electricity, but this old one on the copper landline still worked, because the phone company powered the line, all the way from town. "Mom!" she shouted. "The wall phone works!" Her mom came in with two candles, and Georgia held up the handset like a trophy.

She spun the dial for Mariam's number, listening to the zip of each number as it wound back. "Hello?" Mariam's voice, tinny and surprised. "It's Georgia. I'm on the crazy old wall phone because the power's out. Don't take River Road tomorrow, there's construction." "You sound like you're calling from 1975," Mariam said. "Come early and bring snacks. I want to try dialing it too."

After she hung up, Georgia sat on the kitchen floor by candlelight, drafting a list of everything that still worked without power: the wall phone, the wood stove, the hand-cranked radio. When a cold draft slipped under the back door, she pulled a towel across the gap and grinned at the humming phone on the wall. "You," she told it, "are staying right there."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Sikhism accepts rebirth and karma, but Guru Nanak taught that the body takes birth because of karma while salvation is attained through God's grace.
story:
Austin spread his notes across the kitchen table until they reached the fruit bowl. His presentation was due tomorrow, and the chart in front of him had two neat columns, one for Christianity and one for Sikhism, and the Sikhism column was almost empty.

"You said you'd help," he said when Melia arrived, still holding her bike helmet.

"I said I'd look at it." She dropped the helmet on the counter and pulled out a chair. "Half my family will read this if it goes up on the class wall."

"So is any of it wrong?" He slid the page toward her. He had written that in Sikhism, you are reborn according to your karma, and if your good deeds outweigh your bad ones, you eventually escape the cycle.

Melia tapped the second line with one finger. "That part's wrong."

"How? Karma means deeds. Good deeds, good rebirth. That's like a bank account."

"Simile, not proof." She got up and opened the fridge like she owned the kitchen, then seemed to remember whose kitchen it was. "Sorry. Can I have the yogurt?"

"Take the yogurt. Explain the bank thing."

"Okay, so my nani says it like this." Melia sat back down and peeled the lid. "The body takes birth because of karma."

Austin wrote it down. "Because of karma. So deeds put you in the cycle."

"And rebirth is real, and karma is real. But getting out isn't a payment." She scooped yogurt with the spoon he handed her. "Guru Nanak taught that salvation comes through God's grace. Not through stacking up enough good deeds to buy your way out."

Austin sat back. "Then why do good deeds at all?"

"That was my exact question at Sunday school, and my teacher made me ask my grandfather." She pointed the spoon at him. "He said, you don't do them to get out. That part isn't in your hands."

Austin crossed out half his chart. "So the two columns are more different than I thought. Christianity has judgment and heaven, and Sikhism has the cycle and grace, and they only match a little."

"Which is a better presentation than pretending they match a lot." Melia leaned over his shoulder. "Put the quote in. Ms. Wang likes quotes."

Ms. Wang more than liked quotes; she had called his last topic controversial because he had only presented one side. He printed GURU NANAK at the top of the column, then the line about the body and karma, then salvation through God's grace, and underneath it, in smaller letters, "told to me by Melia Kaur, who learned it from her grandfather." He would document his source properly, the way Ms. Wang had shown them, name and date on the last slide.

"That's actually decent," Melia said.

"I know it's decent." He squared the pages against the table edge and clipped them together. "Eat your yogurt. You're reading the whole thing out loud before you leave."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, most often because the eyeball is slightly too long.
story:
Aurora's new glasses arrived on a Tuesday, and she brought them to school in a case that felt like a secret. At morning break she sat on the low wall by the climbing frame, sliding them on and off, while Arian peered over her shoulder.

"They're extravagant," he said, watching the frames catch the sun. "Like a movie star's."

"Mr. Menon says I'm nearsighted," Aurora said. "Light from faraway stuff focuses in front of my retina instead of right on it. In my case, because my eyeball is a tiny bit too long." She said it the way she'd repeated it to herself on the bus, and Arian nodded as if he'd known it for years.

London flopped down beside them, squinting at the scoreboard at the far end of the field, where somebody had chalked the lunchtime netball tally. "Who won yesterday? I can't read that from here. It's just a smear." Then, without missing a beat, she pulled out her phone and read a message aloud, crisp and clear, from a screen she held a foot from her face.

Aurora sat up straight. Here was the thing she'd been turning over all morning. She could read the tiny print on a cereal box, but before the glasses the board from the back row had been fog. Far away, blurry. Close up, sharp. That was the pattern, and London matched it exactly. If London's eye was even a millimeter too long, then the light from that distant scoreboard would land short of where it needed to be, while the light from a phone an arm's length away would still arrive in the right place. There was only one way to test it.

"Try these," Aurora said, holding out the glasses. "Don't drop them, but try. I want to check something."

London put them on. She blinked, then turned toward the scoreboard, and her mouth fell open. "I can read it. Blue team, six." She spun around, taking in the whole field, the fence, the classroom windows. "Everything's got edges. How did I not know?"

"Because you had nothing to compare it to," Aurora said. "I didn't either, until today."

Arian grinned. "This is going to become one of your anecdotes. 'The day I diagnosed London on the playground.'"

Aurora laughed, but she was already writing a note in her head for London's mum. At lunch London slid the glasses back into Aurora's hand, careful as a returned library book. She'd made her own appointment for Saturday, and she'd written it on her arm in pen so she couldn't lose it.

On the way back inside, Aurora looked up at the water tower three streets away, its legs sharp against the sky for the first time in her life. "Everything's been orbiting me all this year," she said, "and I never even saw it coming."

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: When writing that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF, the order of the letters matters: A matches D, B matches E and C matches F.
story:
The library after school smelled like dust and old glue, and Luke had claimed the table by the window where the radiator actually worked. He spread out his geometry notes, frowned at them, and slid the sheet across to Omer, who had already sharpened two pencils and lined them up like surgical tools.

"Ms. Buchanan handed back our quizzes during homeroom," Omer said. "I got six out of ten on the congruence question. Six. Titan got nine, and he didn't even study." He flattened the quiz on the table with both palms, as if it might blow away. "I'm getting above him on Friday's test or I'm quitting math forever."

Luke leaned in. Omer had drawn two triangles, one labeled ABC and the other DEF, with little ticks showing that two sides and the angle between them matched. He had written "triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF" and circled it. The proof itself looked right to Luke. The ticks were in the right places. The side-angle-side rule, the one they'd drilled all week, seemed satisfied. So where had four marks gone?

Ms. Buchanan passed behind them with a cart of biographies, stopped, and tapped the circled sentence. "Look closely at what you matched to what," she said, and rolled on toward the dilapidated shelves in the back corner, where the spine of a book about ancient Rome had been repaired so many times with tape that it looked like propaganda posters from some cardboard empire.

Luke stared at the sentence until his eyes ached. Look closely at what you matched to what. He picked up Omer's pencil and wrote the letters in a column: A, then B, then C. Under them: D, then E, then F. First letter under first letter, second under second. He read each pair like two kids picking teammates. A matched with D. B matched with E. C matched with F. That was the whole secret hiding in the sentence, the order of the letters doing quiet work that nobody had told them about.

"Wait," Omer whispered. He checked his drawing. His angle marks, the ones with the double arcs, were at B on the first triangle and at F on the second. B was second in his sentence, and F was last. B didn't line up with F at all. B went with E, and his angle sat with E's spot, not F's. "The letters have to be in the same order," Omer said slowly, "or the whole thing says the wrong triangles." He grabbed a fresh sheet and copied the proof, this time writing triangle ACB is congruent to triangle DFE, second letter to second letter, angle to angle, everything locking into place like a zipper.

"Titan's going to walk in Friday thinking he's already won," Omer said, and started investing his remaining pencil lead in a second practice problem. Luke slid his own paper over and copied the column of letters, A above D, B above E, C above F, and drew a box around it. "Show me the next one," he said.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Places, people and routines linked with nicotine use, such as a certain time of day, can become cues that trigger cravings on their own.
story:
The dentist's waiting room had a reputation for being the slowest place in town, and Ruby was starting to believe it. The chairs were lined up under a poster about flossing, the magazine rack was sparse, and the clock over the reception desk ticked like it was being paid by the hour. She had her science presentation folded in her backpack, half finished, due tomorrow: explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway. Her poster had a drawing of a brain with arrows pointing to a spot labeled reward pathway, and under it she had written only one shaky sentence.

"Grandpa, why do you keep jiggling your foot?" she asked.

Her grandfather sat beside her, holding a paper cup of coffee from the machine in the corner. "Habit," he said, and took a sip. Then he set the cup down on the armrest and pushed it an inch away, like it had done something to him.

Ruby watched him. He picked up a magazine, put it down, picked up the coffee, and pushed it away again. That was a pattern, and Ruby liked patterns, even ones she could not explain yet. "You keep doing that with the coffee," she said. "Every time you drink some."

"Every time you drink some," said a voice from the next chair. It was Yoan, from her science class, who had apparently been sitting there the whole time, headphones around his neck. "Sorry. I couldn't help hearing. That's actually really good material."

"For what?" Ruby said.

"Your presentation. Mine's the same topic, nicotine and the reward pathway. Mr. Do says we have to make it real, not just a diagram." Yoan leaned forward. "Your grandpa is basically a live demonstration."

Grandpa laughed, but it was a thin laugh. "I don't think I want to be a demonstration."

Ruby looked at him, at the coffee cup, at the way his fingers drummed the armrest. Something clicked into place, slow and certain, like a lock turning. "You smoked," she said. It wasn't a question. "Before. A long time ago. You quit."

The waiting room went quiet except for the clock. "Forty years ago," Grandpa said finally. "Before your mom was even born." He picked up the coffee again and held it without drinking. "You want to know the strange part? Morning coffee still makes me think of cigarettes. All these years. I quit the cigarettes, but the morning, the coffee, the same chair, the same time of day, they stayed with me. They make me want one, even now."

"That's it," Ruby whispered. She pulled the poster out of her backpack and spread it across her knees. "Nicotine trains the reward pathway, that part I had. But then places, people and routines linked with nicotine use, like a certain time of day, can become cues that trigger cravings all on their own. That's what the coffee is. The coffee is a cue." She wrote the word in big letters and underlined it twice. "Grandpa, can I ask you something? Don't drink any more until I say. Just sit."

He raised an eyebrow but set the cup down.

"Okay. Now drink."

He drank. His fingers stopped drumming for a second, then started again, faster. "Well," he said, staring into the cup. "That's annoying to know."

"It's perfect," Ruby said. "The craving persists even when the nicotine is gone for decades. The cue does it by itself." Yoan was copying her diagram onto the back of his hand, and the receptionist called Grandpa's name through the little window. He stood up, tucking the poster corner back under Ruby's knee where it had curled.

"You owe me one story about your brain," he said, and followed the hygienist through the door, coffee cup left behind on the armrest, still steaming.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
The morning after the talent show, Theodore opened the class blog on the library computer and deleted his post about Mr. Bautista's singing. He had written it in a hurry, thinking it was funny, and now every read of it made his ears go hot. "It's gone," he said to the screen. "Nobody can see it."

"Except everybody already did," Margaret said from the next seat. "Winston printed it." She slid the page across the table. His words were still there, plain as anything, even though the post itself had vanished from the blog. Theodore tried to snatch the paper, but she held it out of reach, and for a moment they were both silent, each waiting for the other to flinch.

At lunch he found Winston in the computer lab. "You printed my post." "The class voted on it," Winston said. "It got shared around before you deleted it. Unanimous, by the way. Everyone thought it was mean." Theodore's plan to argue back was thwarted by the look on Winston's face, so he sat down instead. "It's deleted," he said. "It doesn't exist anymore." Winston spun his chair toward a monitor. "That's what you think. My brother says public pages get copied. There's a thing called the Wayback Machine." He typed the address, then the blog's address. A list of dates appeared. "It's saved more than one trillion web pages. So something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found."

Theodore didn't believe it until he clicked the date. There was the blog, exactly as it had been that morning, and there was his post, sitting on the screen with his name under the title. His stomach dropped. He scrolled down and checked, then checked again, as if the page might change its mind. Deleting had only hidden it from one place, and the copy had been waiting somewhere he had never thought to look. It was like light through a prism, splitting one thing he had done into pieces he couldn't gather back.

He walked to Mr. Bautista's room before the bell. The projector was on, and the humming of the fan filled the quiet. Theodore stood in the doorway with the printed page folded small in his fist. "I wrote something about you," he said. "I deleted it, but I found out it might still be there. I wanted to say I'm sorry before you find it." Mr. Bautista set down his markers and looked at him for a long moment. "Sit down," he said. "Show me."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Laughing along with teasing, even just to fit in, signals approval to the person teasing and tends to encourage them to keep going.
story:
Steam from the pasta pot made the kitchen window fog up until the backyard lights blurred into soft yellow smears, and Edouard watched the moisture condense into slow drops while he pushed peas around his plate.

"So the shop's doing all right?" asked Mr. Ramos, their neighbour, who came for dinner every second Thursday and always brought the same hard rolls.

"Revenue's up since spring," Edouard's father said. "Kade's father says the same about his hardware store, so it's not just us."

At the name, Edouard's stomach tightened. Kade. At lunch that day, Kade had done his impression of Inara's sneeze, that honking noise she couldn't help, and Edouard had laughed. He hadn't wanted to. Everyone at the table had been laughing, and it had seemed easier to join in than to sit there like a stone. Inara had packed up her lunch and moved to the empty table by the window.

"Edouard's got a face on him tonight," his little brother announced. "Maybe he's thinking about his math test. Thirty-eight percent, wasn't it?"

Their father chuckled. Edouard's brother grinned, then glanced quickly at their father, checking, like a fisherman watching a bobber.

"Thirty-eight," the brother repeated. "Out of a hundred."

Their father laughed again, longer this time, and the brother sat up straighter, loading the next one. Edouard saw it plainly now, the way he hadn't seen it at lunch: the glance after every joke. The laugh wasn't just noise. It was a green light, and his brother was driving straight through it, one joke after another, because the audience kept waving him on.

Edouard tried an experiment. He kept his fork moving and his face flat, and he said, evenly, "You went through my bag."

Their father's smile faded. He set down his glass. "That's his to tell, not yours."

The brother looked at their father, found no bobber moving, and shrugged and reached for the bread. There was no third joke. Edouard sat with that for a moment, turning it over. A laugh, even a fake one, even a small one, told the teaser to keep going. Quiet and steady told him something else. It seemed almost too simple, but he had watched it work at his own dinner table in the space of four minutes.

The next day at lunch, Kade started the sneeze impression before Edouard even sat down. A couple of kids at the end of the table giggled, and Kade's eyes flicked toward them, checking, waiting.

Edouard didn't laugh and didn't yell. He set his tray down next to Inara's and said, "Sit with us, Inara. You're the only one here who actually finished the history reading."

She slid her bag over. The giggling at the end of the table ran out of air like a record winding down, and Kade, finding no green light anywhere, picked up his sandwich and ate it.

"Page ninety-four was wild," Inara said.

"Tell me everything," Edouard said, and opened his milk.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
story:
The night before the Seder, Ariana found her six-year-old cousin behind the couch, whispering into a pillow. "Why is this night different from all other nights?" the pillow was asked, in a voice smaller than a mouse wearing earmuffs. Jonah had been practicing the Four Questions all week, because at a Passover Seder, the meal where everyone retells the story of the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks them, and at this table that job belonged to Jonah.

"Are you hiding from the matzah?" Ariana asked, crouching down.

"I'm hiding from twenty-six eyeballs," Jonah said. "Grandma invited extra people. I counted."

Ariana didn't think the problem was the eyeballs. She'd watched him recite to the dog flawlessly, then freeze when their uncle walked in. It wasn't memorizing that scared him. It was being watched. She had a theory, and a way to test it. "Do the first question for me, right here, right now," she said. "Just me. One pair of eyeballs."

He did it, wobbling only once. "See?" she said. "Your brain is like a little turbine. It spins fine until too many people pile coal into it." Jonah laughed at that, which was the plan, and then Ariana said, "Tomorrow, when you stand up, find me. I'll be your one pair."

The next evening the table stretched past the dilapidated old leaf they only used twice a year, the one that wobbled like a loose tooth. Jonah sat between Grandpa and Ariana's friend Kacey, who had never been to a Seder before and had already asked three questions of her own, which was ironic, as Thierry pointed out from across the table. The candles were lit, the first cup poured, and everyone turned toward Jonah.

He stood up. His eyes swept the room, twenty-six eyeballs wide as soup bowls. Ariana could practically hear the turbine stuttering. She leaned forward and mouthed, "Just me." She tapped her own eyeballs, then pointed at herself, then knocked over the water glass, which made Kacey gasp and Grandpa rescue the Haggadah with the speed of a much younger man.

Everyone laughed, including Jonah, and something in his shoulders let go. He took a breath and asked why this night was different from all other nights, all four questions in order, wobbling only at the same spot he always did, and nobody minded, because by then the room was too busy rescuing parsley to notice.

"You did that on purpose," Kacey whispered to Ariana, helping mop the water.

"I have no idea what you mean," Ariana said, and passed her the towel.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
story:
Theo stood in his grandfather's kitchen holding a knife the way you'd hold a sword, which his grandfather said was exactly wrong. "Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Grandpa said. "Knuckles forward. The blade rides against them and your fingertips stay out of trouble." Theo bent his fingers until they looked like a crab checking under a rock. Then he chopped, and the half onion jumped and rolled and one piece flew off the counter entirely.

"That piece is escaping," Theo said.

"Let it go. It has dreams." Grandpa slid the cutting board closer. "Again. Slow is fine. Slow is actually fast, because you keep all ten fingers."

The problem, as Theo saw it, was that Saturday was the family dinner, and he had promised Mariah and Ewan a real pasta sauce made from scratch, not the stuff from a jar. Grandpa's kitchen had one of those old counters with a wobble in it, barely big enough to accommodate one cook, let alone three kids and a pot of boiling water. Theo had tested the wobble that morning by pressing on the corner, and the whole surface tipped a little, like a seesaw with a grudge. He decided the solution was to keep the knife on the far side, on the flat part, and to chop with his claw grip and the onion pulled close.

The onion, once he got going, was almost pretty. The papery skin was translucent, thin enough to read a note through, and the layers underneath shone white and wet. His eyes burned anyway. "I'm not crying," he announced when Ewan arrived. "I'm leaking strategically."

"Sure," said Ewan, who was washing tomatoes at the sink and had found, on one of them, a fat green larva curled on a leaf. "You're leaking strategically while I guard this little guy. Mariah, come look, he'sadorable."

Mariah came in carrying basil from the garden, took one look at Theo's puffy eyes, and laughed so hard she had to put the basil down. Then things went wrong fast. Mariah reached across the counter for a bowl, her elbow landed on the wobbly end, the counter tipped, and the knife slid toward the edge. Theo's hand shot out to grab it before his brain caught up. Grandpa's voice came from the doorway, quick and calm: "Never catch a falling knife. Step back and let it drop." Theo jumped back and the knife hit the floor, bounced once, and lay there, handle up, harmless.

Everybody stood very still. "So that's a rule," Theo said. "If a knife starts to fall, you let it fall." His heart was thumping, but his fingers were all still attached, which he checked twice. Grandpa nodded and picked the knife up by the handle.

"Cook's rule number one," Grandpa said. "Now. Who's going to accommodate this larva with a new home in the garden, and who's going back to their onion?"

Theo picked up the knife, curled his fingers into the claw, and got back to chopping.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
story:
Sofia slid into the middle seat of the family car with her ears still ringing from the argument she had lost. The objective had been simple: convince her parents to let her skip this trip and stay with Daphnee for the long weekend. Instead she was buckled between her little brother, Marco, and a bag of snacks, watching their street shrink in the mirror.

"It's only two hours to the airport," her mother said, "and then the flight is three more. You can text Daphnee from the plane."

Marco, who was four, was already chewing on the strap of his booster seat, which was his way of concealing how nervous he felt. Sofia knew the signs. He had never flown before, and last night she had heard him whisper to their father that airplanes made his friend's ears "pop like bubble wrap."

At the gate, Sofia spotted Imran from her class in the same line, holding a giant pretzel. "Flight to Denver?" he said. "Same. My ears are going to be destroyed. Last summer I thought my head would cave in when we landed."

"Mine too," Sofia admitted. "But it always stops after a minute."

Imran shrugged. "My grandma just makes us suck on candy the whole time down. Works, I guess."

That stuck in Sofia's head during the flight. Candy, and on the way to the car that morning her mother had kept saying, "Swallow, baby, swallow," when Marco cried on the hills. Swallowing. Why would swallowing matter for ears? Ears and throats weren't even the same part. She turned it over while Marco watched a movie, while the seatbelt sign lit up, while the plane tipped its nose and started down.

Then Marco started screaming. The pressure had hit him, and he clawed at his ears and howled. Their mother dug frantically through the diaper bag, but the snack pouches were all empty, packed in the checked luggage by mistake. Sofia grabbed the juice box she had saved, stabbed the straw through the foil, and pushed it into his hands. He gulped, hiccupped, and stopped crying almost at once. A minute later he reached for it again, took another long swallow, and sighed like a much older person.

"It's the swallowing," Sofia said to Imran across the aisle, amazed. "Somehow it opens the Eustachian tubes, and that lets air into the middle ear. That's what relieves the pressure you feel when the plane descends." She said it out loud mostly to hear whether it sounded true, and it did.

The plane dropped through a layer of cloud. Sofia swallowed hard, felt a small click somewhere deep in her ear, and the pressure let go. Marco drained the last of the juice and announced, "Again," which was the first full sentence he had managed in an hour. The landing gear came down with a roar. Sofia looked at the empty juice box and then at Imran, who was holding out a piece of gum. "Trade you," he said, "for one candy at the car rental counter."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
story:
The last box Hannah carried into the new house had no label at all, just a strip of faded tape and a dent in one corner. She set it down in the hallway between a stack marked KITCHEN in her mother's handwriting and one marked BASEMENT, and she wondered which room her bedsheets were in. Outside, the August air hung humid over the moving truck, and her father was still arguing quietly with the driver about the bill.

In her old town, she had spent the last evening with Ireland and Scarlet on the porch steps. "You have to promise you'll label everything," Ireland had said, holding out a marker like it was a formal ceremony. Scarlet had laughed, but Ireland was serious about systems, about the way things ought to be done. Hannah had taken the marker and labeled four boxes, and then they had gone inside for pizza, and she had packed the rest in a rush the next morning. Now it was dark, the first night in a strange house, and her bed was a bare mattress.

She opened the unlabeled box first. Books, a lamp shade, one sneaker. She opened a second. Winter coats. The hallway floor vanished under shredded paper. She stood there with her hands on her hips and thought about the boxes Ireland had labeled, the ones marked HANNAH'S ROOM, and how those had taken her five minutes to unpack on moving day in fourth grade, because she had carried each one straight upstairs and known what was inside before she opened it. The unlabeled ones hid their contents, and she could not see what was where without cutting tape and digging.

"Did you find the sheets?" her father called from the kitchen. His voice was careful, the way it had been all week, as if one wrong word might make her oppose the whole move out loud. She hadn't argued yet, and he seemed to be waiting for it.

"One more box," she called back, though she had already opened six. In the seventh, under a rolled-up poster, she found the sheets, wrinkled and smelling of cardboard. She made the bed in the dark because she hadn't figured out which switch worked the ceiling light yet.

The next morning she walked to school, and in third period Ms. Aziz handed out index cards and asked everyone to write their name and one thing they wanted her to know. Hannah thought about the question for a long moment. Then she wrote: "I moved here yesterday. My friend Ireland says to label every box with the room it belongs in and what's inside, so you can carry it straight to the right place. I'm going to do that next time, and there better not be a next time." Ms. Aziz read it at the end of class, stopped at Hannah's desk on her way back, and tapped the card. "Someone organized," she said. "Come meet two other organized people at lunch. They sit by the window."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and nervous thirteen-year-olds, and Ryder was one of them. He had made it to the final three of the school spelling bee, and the only thing standing between him and the trophy was Blake, who had studied the entire dictionary twice, and Huxley, who was, honestly, just lucky.
