Mr. Morin, who ran the library and the bee, adjusted the microphone and said, "Ryder, your word is 'subterranean.'"

Ryder started strong. "S. U. B. T. E. R." Then his brain, which liked to simulate disaster scenarios, played one out in full: he saw the word on a page, and the page said the next part was A-I-N, not the A-N-I-A-N his mouth was about to say. He froze halfway, one letter from the cliff edge.

He remembered something his older cousin had told him after watching the Scripps bee on television, the nationals, the real thing. "You can start over," she'd said, munching popcorn. "Say the whole word again from the beginning. But if you change even one letter you already said, that's a misspelling. It counts as wrong." So the rule was simple and cruel at the same time: restart freely, but the letters already out of your mouth are locked in place, like posts in a fence.

Ryder took a breath and tried it. "Subterranean. S. U. B. T. E. R. R. A. N. E. A. N. Subterranean." He had kept every said letter in order and simply marched on. Mr. Morin nodded, and somewhere in the bleachers Huxley whispered, "He paused for like a year and still got it. That's basically cheating with extra steps."

Then came the twist. Mr. Morin turned to Blake with the word "constitution," and Blake, who could spell it in his sleep, rushed so fast he said "C. O. N. S. T. I. T. U. C..." and then heard it. He tried to fix it. "T. I. T. I. O. N." A murmur went through the gym. Mr. Morin shook his head gently. "You changed a letter you'd already said. I'm sorry, Blake. That's a misspelling."

Blake stared at the microphone as if it had personally betrayed him, and Huxley stood up from his seat to spell next. Ryder watched, doing the arithmetic in his head: if Huxley missed, the round was his. But if Huxley got his word, they'd go another round, and Ryder's legs were already doing a nervous equivalent of jelly. Huxley squinted, spelled "dossier" flawlessly, and sat back down with a grin that meant war.

Mr. Morin straightened his cards. "Ryder, next word. 'Rendezvous.'" Ryder stepped up to the mic, and behind him, Blake whispered just loud enough, "Don't pause like a year this time."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
story:
James had been practicing the same eight measures for a week, and every time he played them at Mr. Nur's studio, they sounded wrong. The sheet music had a long sideways triangle under the notes, opening wider toward the right, and James had been ignoring it the way he ignored most of the pencil marks his little sister drew on his homework.

"Play it again," said Maliyah, who took her lesson right after his and had stayed to listen. "But this time, watch the triangle."

"It's just decoration," James said. "Like a haircut for the music."

Maliyah laughed so hard she knocked over the stack of method books by the window. Mr. Nur, who was tuning something in the back room, called out, "Whatever falls, someone articulates an apology to it." He was always saying odd things like that.

James started the eight measures again. On the fourth beat, Maliyah clapped her hands over her ears in an exaggerated way, then cupped them forward like satellite dishes, then covered them again. He stopped. "What are you doing?"

"I'm showing you what I hear. Loud, then quiet, then loud again. It's like a door slamming." She pointed at the triangle. "That thing isn't decoration. My cousin calls it a crescendo, and a crescendo means gradually getting louder. The opposite one, getting smaller at the end, is a diminuendo, gradually getting softer. Gradually. Not all at once."

James looked at the shape again. It started as a thin point on the left and widened as it moved right. Thin, then wide. Quiet, then loud, and all the space in between. He had been playing the whole passage at one volume, medium and flat, like a robot reading a grocery list.

He tried it with the new idea. He began the first measure barely touching the keys, so soft the notes felt like whispers, then grew through the second and third measures until the last measure rang out. He did the reverse on the next line, where the triangle shrank, letting the sound sink down until it almost wasn't there. His brain felt the way it did when a math problem suddenly opened up, like a neuron had flipped on a light switch somewhere behind his eyes.

"Like a wave coming in and going out," Maliyah said quietly.

Mr. Nur appeared in the doorway, drying his hands on a towel. "That was not the conventional flat delivery you gave me last week, James. That was music. Do it once more, and this time I'm getting my coffee, because I intend to enjoy it."

James set his fingers on the starting keys and took a breath.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Two climate graphs can only be compared by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale; otherwise a short bar may stand for more rain.
story:
Antoine spread two climate graphs across the library table like a detective laying out evidence. One showed a desert city, all tiny rainfall bars and a temperature line that crawled along the top. The other showed a tropical city in the rainforest, where the bars looked like a parade of green skyscrapers. His homework said to compare them, and Ms. Han had promised that whoever did the best job would get their graph displayed at the front of the room, which Antoine secretly wanted more than he would ever admit out loud.

"Move over," said Tatum, dropping her backpack on the chair beside him. "Cyrus and I are having an emergency." Cyrus slid into the seat across the table, holding a third graph like it had personally insulted him.

"Tell him," Cyrus said, jabbing a finger at his paper. "My city is wetter. Look at these bars. They're taller than Antoine's rainforest bars. Mine go almost to the top of the page."

"Your city is in a desert," Tatum said. "I've seen actual cactus postcards from there. Deserts are dry. That's basically their whole personality."

"Then why are my bars taller, genius?"

Antoine leaned over, expecting to settle it in two seconds, but the bars really were taller. He frowned. Somewhere in the back of his mind, a small alarm bell rang, the kind that meant something didn't fit. He turned the desert graph sideways, squinted at it, and nearly knocked over his pencil doing it.

While Tatum and Cyrus kept arguing, Antoine pulled a folded note out of his pocket. Tatum had slipped it to him in the hallway that morning. It said, in her loopy handwriting: "P.S. I already claimed the seat next to you at the library. Don't get any ideas, it's just because you actually do the reading." He read it again, grinned, and wrote underneath: "Noted. Bring your own pencil next time, freeloader." He slid it back across the table. Tatum read it, snorted, and bumped his elbow on purpose, which messed up his temperature line, which he pretended to be furious about for exactly four seconds.

Then he went back to the mystery. He looked at the rainforest graph, then the desert graph, then held them side by side. The bars couldn't both tell the truth, unless the graphs weren't playing by the same rules. He bent close to the rainfall side of each one, past the bars themselves, to the little numbers running up the edge of the paper. The rainforest graph counted by tens. The desert graph counted by hundreds. He checked twice, tracing the numbers with his pencil tip, because it seemed too sneaky to be real.

"Ha!" Antoine said, a little too loud for the library. A man at the next table gave him a look, and Antoine shrank down and whispered, "Your graphs have different scales. Tatum, read the side of Cyrus's graph. Out loud, quietly."

Tatum squinted at the numbers. "It says two hundred at the top. Yours says sixty."

"So my shortest bar," Cyrus said slowly, "could actually be more rain than your tallest bar?"

"Exactly," Antoine said. "You can only compare them by bar height if the rainfall axes use the same scale." He flipped to the back of his handout, found a blank grid, and started redrawing both cities on one set of numbers so the comparison would be honest. Tatum helped him rule the lines, and Cyrus, still muttering about betrayal by graph paper, checked the axis numbers on every climate chart the library had in the rack, one by one, like a customs officer.

By the time the librarian announced closing, Antoine's redrawn graph was finished, with the desert's little stubs dwarfed by the tropical city's towering bars, all on the same scale. "Ms. Han is going to frame this," Tatum said. "You know she keeps a scholarship folder for kids who show their work, right?"

Antoine rolled up the graph, tucked it under his arm, and held the door for both of them. "Cyrus," he said, "you owe me a postcard from that desert."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
story:
Victor had forty minutes before the library closed and his science homework was still blank. Mr. Pham had already walked past his table twice, tapping the clock, which did nothing to accelerate his thinking. The assignment asked for one claim backed by tested evidence and one story about a single person's experience, and Victor had written neither.

Then Noemie slid into the chair across from him and held up her phone. "Look at this. Kids who eat blueberries get better grades. It's a real headline."

"Then I should eat blueberries," Victor said. "All of them."

Brynley leaned over from the next table. "My cousin eats blueberries every morning and he failed geography twice."

"So one guy," Noemie said. "That's just a story about one person."

Victor stared at the headline. Something about it itched. He grabbed a scrap paper and drew two arrows going up side by side, one labeled blueberries, one labeled grades. "Okay, they rise together. But wait." He remembered an example his older sister had mocked once, some article about summer. "Ice cream sales and sunburns. Those go up together too, but ice cream doesn't burn you. Hot weather causes both."

"Correlation," Brynley said, snapping her gum. "Two things moving together doesn't mean one caused the other. My mom says that constantly."

"So maybe the blueberry kids have something else in common," Victor said. He flipped the scrap paper over and started a list. Richer families? More breakfast? Parents who make them do homework? He couldn't tell from the headline. The article gave no numbers, no test, no control group, nothing but a survey.

"That's the problem," Noemie said. "A survey isn't a test. My brother is impulsive, he'd read that headline and buy a crate of blueberries tonight."

"He'd have a great reputation as the healthiest kid failing math," Brynley said.

Victor laughed, then looked at the clock. Twelve minutes. He wrote fast: the claim he trusted was the one about vaccines from his textbook, tested on huge groups with evidence behind it; the blueberry headline was a claim wearing evidence's jacket. He scribbled the difference down just as Mr. Pham appeared at his elbow.

"Five minutes," Mr. Pham said. "And no, I am not checking your paper for you. Again."

Victor's pen raced across the last line. Then Noemie tapped her phone screen. "There's a follow-up study," she said slowly. "It says they did test it. Actual testing." She looked up at him. "Guess what it found."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Stella stood at the smoothie counter at Riverside Mall, holding her phone so Isa could see the screen. "Look," she said. "I posted that photo of us at the fountain last Saturday, and this morning a guy named Marcus liked it. I've never even met him. My account is private."

"That's weird," Isa said, sucking the last of her mango smoothie through the straw with a noise like a dying balloon. "Private means strangers can't see it, right?"

"That's what I thought." Stella scrolled. Marcus had three hundred followers and a profile picture of somebody's motorcycle. She'd accepted his follow request months ago because they had eleven mutual friends and she hadn't thought about it since. Was that it? Being private was like locking the front door, but anyone already inside could still carry things out.

"I need to test this," she said. Dan arrived then, lugging a shopping bag from the game store, and Stella explained. "I'll post something only followers can see, and I'll ask Priya's cousin to check. She follows me but I don't know her at all."

"You're running a spy experiment in a mall food court," Dan said. "That's kind of radical."

Stella posted a photo of her smoothie with a tiny paper umbrella in it and sent Priya's cousin a message: can you see my last post? Ten minutes later the answer came back: yep, saw it, saved it too, cute umbrella. Stella felt her stomach drop, in the way it did when a rollercoaster started.

"So it's like this," she said slowly, tapping the table with each point. "Private limits who can see my posts. Strangers scrolling around can't. But anyone I already accepted as a follower can still copy or share whatever they see." Priya's cousin had barely known Stella, and Stella had barely known Marcus, and there he was, liking a photo he should never have laid eyes on. Unless. Maybe someone had forwarded it to him? She asked Priya later, by the fountain, and Priya admitted her cousin did sometimes repost things to a group chat. That would refute nothing, actually; it fit perfectly. It proved it.

"It's not fair," Isa said. "It's like the account is private except for the part that isn't."

Stella laughed, a short, startled sound. She opened her follower list, two hundred and sixty names long, and started removing the ones she couldn't put a face to. Marcus went first, then a girl called sunset_lord, then eleven others. It felt like a tiny rebellion, sweeping out strangers from a room she'd thought was locked.

"Hey," Dan said, peering over her shoulder. "You're deleting people with your thumb. You should put that on your resume. Professional bouncer."

"Professional smoothie bouncer," Stella said, and removed number fourteen.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described his model of argument, including claim, data and warrant, in his 1958 book 'The Uses of Argument'.
story:
Andrew unfolded the note that Auston had passed him under the table, folded into a square so small it looked like a suspicious mint. "Your second point has no warrant," it read. "It's just a claim wearing a trench coat, pretending to be an argument. Fix it or we lose to Soraya. P.S. she brought a graph." Andrew crumpled the note, uncrumpled it, and read it again, because unfortunately Auston was right. Andrew had a claim, that school lunches should be free, and he had evidence, a study showing that kids in impoverished districts scored higher when meals were provided. What he did not have was the middle part, the bridge that explained why the evidence proved the claim. The timer said four minutes until the round began.

He leaned over to Auston and whispered, "Okay, but who even invented the word warrant? Why is it called that? It sounds like something a judge signs before raiding a house." Auston shrugged with his whole body, the way he did when he wanted credit for shrugging. But the girl at the next table, waiting for her own round, looked up from her flow pad. "The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described his model of argument, including claim, data and warrant," she said. "It's in his book from 1958, The Uses of Argument." She said it the way you'd recite a phone number you'd dialed a thousand times, then went back to her pad.

Andrew stared at his own notes. 1958. A British philosopher had sat down and mapped out the exact thing Andrew was failing to do, so long ago that his grandmother could have read it as a kid. He tested the idea right there, muttering under his breath. "Free lunches improve learning, that's the claim. The study shows scores went up, that's the data. The warrant is the rule underneath: if kids aren't hungry, they can focus." He tried it backward too, like a proof. If the rule were false, if hunger helped concentration, the evidence would mean nothing. The bridge was the whole point. "Auston," he whispered, "my trench coat has a body in it now."

"Time," called Ms. Chen, the tab-room official, and the round began. Soraya went first, and she did bring a graph, a big pink one with a line climbing like a squirrel up a fence. Andrew listened, and to his delight her second point was exactly what his had been that morning: a claim, a pile of numbers, and a gap in the middle wide enough to drive the debate bus through. When his turn came, he stood, took a breath, and walked across the bridge he had finally built. "My opponent's data shows the median attendance rose," he said. "But she never tells you why that proves her claim. I'll comply with her numbers and still show she's wrong, because numbers without a warrant are just a pink graph wearing a trench coat."

Soraya's mouth fell open, then curved into a grudging grin. Auston passed him another tiny square of paper. Andrew unfolded it to find a single drawing: a trench coat, crossed out, with a small crown drawn on top. "Nice crown," Andrew whispered. "You're wearing it," Auston whispered back.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
story:
Dylan spotted Juniper at the third picnic table by the duck pond, exactly where she always sat on Saturdays, headphones on, sketching the geese. He hadn't spoken to her in five weeks, not since he joined the swim team and she started spending every afternoon in the art room. For a while they'd texted, but the messages got shorter and shorter, like a battery dying. Now he stood behind a sycamore tree, holding his notebook, trying to make his feet move.

His instinct said turn around. Instead he crossed the grass and set the notebook on the table.

She pulled out one earbud. "What."

"Last night I found this study," he said. "From 2015. It followed 573 friendships that started in seventh grade." He flipped the notebook open to where he'd copied the numbers. "The friends who were less alike were the ones more likely to see the friendship end."

Juniper set down her pencil. "So what's that mean, we're done?"

"It means we used to be the same and now we're not, so it's like the whole thing is set up to break." He tapped the page. "But it's not a rule. It's what usually happens."

"Comforting."

Braylon jogged past with his soccer ball, waved, and kept going. Dylan waited until he was out of earshot. "I've been thinking about it all week. The study says alike friends stick. So I made a list." He turned the page. On it were two columns, so symmetrical they looked mirrored. Her side: geese, charcoal drawing, the pond. His side: swimming, the pond, underwater photos on his phone.

Her eyes went down the page and stopped. "The pond's on both sides."

"I take pictures of the water when I'm training. You draw what's floating on it. Same water."

Juniper studied her sketch, then his phone screen, then the pond itself, where two geese were drifting side by side. She was quiet for long enough that he started folding the notebook closed. Then she slid it back open with one finger.

"Show me the photos."

He sat down on the bench across from her and scrolled. There was the pond at sunrise, mist on the surface. There was a goose reflected in the shallows, its image wobbling. She leaned in, and he saw her fingers twitch the way they did when she wanted a pencil.

"That reflection," she said. "I've tried to draw that maybe ten times. The light's never right."

"I can get you more of them. Morning practice is at six." He hesitated. "I could bring you the best ones. You could, I don't know, make them into something."

"Deal," she said, and handed him her spare pencil. "Draw a frame around this one. Something simple. Maybe two lines, matching."

He drew them slow and careful, one on each side, and she watched the whole time.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
story:
Charles sat cross-legged in the reading nook by the upstairs window with his copy of The Monkey's Paw open on his knees, a yellow sticky note curling off the cover. Tomorrow Ms. Walker would call on three people to explain foreshadowing and symbolism, and he had promised himself he would not be the one staring at his desk. The problem was that every time he read the story, the clues seemed to hide from him, like they were part of the game too.

"Text me the answer," Cheikh had said at lunch, but Charles had shaken his head. He actually wanted to understand it. So when Farrah came over that evening, carrying her own battered copy, he pulled her into the nook before she could even take off her shoes.

"Read the part where the soldier visits," he said. "The guest, whatever his name is."

"Sergeant-Major Morris," Farrah said, flipping pages. She found the spot and read aloud, her voice dropping lower for effect. The old soldier tells the White family plainly that the paw's wishes have brought terrible results. Then, before anyone can stop him, he throws the thing into the fire.

Charles sat up so fast he banged his elbow on the bookshelf. "There. Right there. That's the warning. Before the family makes a single wish, he tells them wishes end badly and tries to burn the paw." He grabbed his pencil. "So anything bad that happens after, the story warned you first. That's foreshadowing, right? The hints come early and pay off later."

Farrah frowned at the page. "Okay, but then the father rescues it from the fire. Why would the story do that if the paw is dangerous?"

Charles chewed the end of his pencil. He thought about the chess game early in the story, where the father takes wild risks nobody expects to work. He thought about the cold wind rattling the window while the fire crackled. "Maybe the paw symbolizes greed," he said slowly. "Wanting things you shouldn't reach for. Morris throws it away, and the family pulls it back out. They choose it."

"So the warning only works if they ignore it," Farrah said.

"Which they do." Charles wrote: The soldier's warning is foreshadowing. The paw rescued from the fire symbolizes the family's greed. He read the sentence twice, then underlined it. "Ms. Walker always says we have to say what the clues suggest, not just find them."

Farrah grinned and closed her book. "You realize you just did the whole assignment."

"It wasn't luck," Charles said, though it partly was, the way the pieces had suddenly lined up. "I made myself slow down at the fire scene instead of rushing to the scary part." He thought of Cheikh, who had skipped the reading entirely and planned to guess tomorrow. The probability of guessing right on Ms. Walker's questions seemed close to zero.

"What about Cheikh?" Farrah asked.

Charles pulled out his phone and typed a message: Read the scene where Morris visits. Meet me here at seven. It was not going to be a vain effort, he decided, because Cheikh liked scary stories once he actually opened them.

He set the phone on the windowsill, where it buzzed almost at once. "On my way," the screen said. Charles moved his sneakers off the cushion to make room.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
story:
Antoine laced his shoes against the wall of the gymnasium while the coach dragged a bag of volleyballs toward the net. Tryouts started in ten minutes, and his objective was simple: make the team, any position, even bench warmer. Then Lucia walked in carrying a gym bag, and the whispering started near the bleachers.

"She's in the wrong gym," someone said. "Girls' tryouts are Thursday."

Lucia heard it and kept walking. She set her bag down two feet from Antoine and began stretching, calm as anything. "There is no girls' volleyball team," she said to him, not to the whisperers. "There's only this one."

Antoine had seen her play in gym class. Her serve was better than his, honestly, and she never missed a free ball. But he knew how the rest of the week would go if people decided she didn't belong. The coach would find reasons, small ones, like "not enough spots" or "you're too short," even though half the returning players were shorter. He had a feeling the coach was biased, but a feeling wasn't proof, and you couldn't argue with a feeling in front of thirty kids.

The coach blew the whistle and split them into squads. Lucia landed on Antoine's side, which gave him a front-row seat, so to speak. She passed everything clean. During the water break, he sat beside her on the bleachers and said, "If he cuts you, are you going to fight it?"

"I already know the rule," Lucia said. "It's called Title IX. A law from 1972. It bans discrimination based on sex in schools that get federal money, and it applies to sports programs."

Antoine turned that over. So if there was no girls' team, and the school took federal money, then the school had to let her try out, and cutting her just for being a girl would be against the law. That part he could work out himself. What he couldn't see was whether the coach would break the rule anyway, quietly, disguised as a numbers game. That was the hidden thing. You couldn't see a biased decision directly; you could only see the excuse it wore.

So he tested it. At the end of the session, the coach posted a list of names called back for day two, and Lucia's name was missing, along with four boys who had honestly played poorly. Antoine copied the list onto his hand with a pen. Then he walked over to Mr. Asante, who taught social studies and was locking the equipment room across the hall.

"Mr. Asante, if a tryout list looked unfair, how would someone prove it?"

Mr. Asante squinted at the smudged ink on Antoine's palm. "You'd compare the numbers," he said. "Who got cut, who kept their spots, and what the stats say. Coaches keep everything. It's the paper trail that does the talking."

Antoine spent that evening at his desk with a notebook, two columns, crossing out what the coach said against what Antoine had actually watched happen. Lucia had outplayed three boys who made the list. The pattern held up. The next morning he found Lucia at her locker and slid the notebook across. "This transports the whole argument for us," he said. "Take it to the principal, not the coach. The coach is the one being accused."

The principal read the notebook, made one phone call, and by afternoon the tryout list on the gym door had a new line added in ballpoint at the bottom: Lucia Marsh, day two.

Thursday she out-served the top returner twice in a row. From the sideline Antoine could hear her say, between points, "That one's for the paper trail."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The banner over the picnic table read "Welcome Home, Nagypapa," and Anais had been assigned to keep the candles away from the paper decorations because, as Lili's mother put it, tissue paper was extremely flammable and the wind kept picking up. It was Lili's family gathering, really, but Lili had invited her, and Anais had said yes before checking with her own mother, who had sighed and said fine, be back by eight.

Lili's grandfather had arrived that morning from a town Anais couldn't pronounce, and now he sat at the head of the table signing a big white card that everyone was passing around. When it came back to Lili, she frowned at it and slid it across the tablecloth to Anais. "Look. He signed it wrong. He put his own name in the wrong place."

Anais read the signature. Where everyone else had written a first name and then a last name, he had written something reversed, the family name sitting first, like a door opened from the wrong side. "Maybe he's tired," Anais said. "He flew all night." But that didn't sit right with her, because tired people misspell things or forget things; they don't usually flip them, and the letters were careful and even. She started watching him instead of guessing. When Lili's cousin handed him a get-well card to sign for a neighbor, he signed it the same way, family name first, without hesitating, as if the order were natural to him.

Anais tested a third idea on the guest book by the drinks table, where people had written their names for the reunion. She flipped back through the pages. Every person in the family had signed first name then family name, except one cousin who had doodled a cat, and except Nagypapa, twice, both times with the family name leading. It wasn't a mistake, she realized, because mistakes are scattered, and this was a pattern. He wrote his name the way he had always written it, which meant the order wasn't wrong in his language at all.

She went to find Lili, who was trying to delegate the candle-watching to her little brother and getting nowhere. "Your grandpa didn't make a mistake," Anais said. "In Hungarian, the family name comes first." Lili squinted at her. "Hungarian? Like Hungary?" "That's where he's from, isn't it? It's the same order they use in Chinese and Japanese and Korean names. Mr. Reddy told us that in September, when we did the name cards." Lili's face changed slowly, the way it did when she was rechecking a math answer and finding it right after all.

They brought the card back to Nagypapa together, and Lili pointed at the signature and asked him something in a mixture of English and gestures. He laughed, a dry sound like paper crumpling, and tapped the family name with one finger and said it clearly, then tapped the given name. Lili's cousin translated a little, and between the three of them they pieced it together: he had signed it the proper way, the way it would appear on every official paper he had ever owned, and he had not thought to change it just because he was here now. Lili said, "So when you write to me, it'll look like that?" and he nodded and patted her hand twice.

Later, when the candles were finally lit and somebody's uncle had nearly set a napkin on fire, Lili stood beside Anais watching the old man tell a story with his whole body, arms wide, everyone leaning in even though most of them couldn't follow the words. Anais understood that she had solved the puzzle of the card, but that there was a bigger thing she hadn't solved: the forty years and the ocean that sat between Lili's grandfather and everyone at that table, which no signature order could bridge. Lili leaned her head briefly against Anais's shoulder, then straightened up and called across the yard, "Nagypapa, say my name. Write it your way."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A ball that rolls 3 meters in 2 seconds has an average speed of 1.5 meters per second.
story:
Joshua stood at the top of the skate park bowl with a tennis ball in one hand, a tape measure in the other, and a plan that Landyn kept insisting was ridiculous.

"You're at a skate park," Landyn said. "There are ramps. There are rails. And you want to roll a ball on the flat part and draw a graph."

"It's for Mr. Ahmed's science homework," Joshua said. "Distance and time. I have to measure how fast something rolls and put it on a distance-time graph, and my kitchen floor is too short."

Violette arrived with a stopwatch and a clipboard, which meant she was taking this more seriously than either of them. "Where do we measure from?" she asked.

Joshua dragged his tape measure along the smooth concrete beside the bowl, marking three meters with a piece of chalk. The park was sparse that morning, just one older skater carving the far end, so they had the flat stretch to themselves. "Ball starts at this line," he said, chalking an X. "Landyn, you stand at the three-meter mark and yell when it crosses. Violette, you time it."

"On three," Violette said. "One, two, three."

Joshua released the ball with a gentle push. It wobbled, curved a little, and crossed Landyn's feet.

"Two seconds!" Violette called out.

Joshua wrote it down and then stared at his paper. Three meters, two seconds. He chewed his pencil. Something didn't match his guess, because he'd been sure a slow roll like that was closer to one meter per second.

"So what's the speed?" Landyn asked, peering over his shoulder.

"I have to divide," Joshua said. "Three meters divided by two seconds." He worked it out in the margin. "One point five meters per second. Huh. Faster than I thought."

"That's average speed," Violette said. "For the whole trip."

They tried again to be sure, and again the ball took two seconds, like it was cooperating. Joshua plotted the point on his graph paper: two seconds along the bottom, three meters up the side. Then they rolled the ball harder, and it covered the three meters in one second flat, which gave him a second point, and a steeper line when he connected them.

"The harder roll makes a steeper line," Joshua said, mostly to himself.

"Obviously," said Landyn, who had not drawn a single thing.

"Then help me instead of standing there looking cool," Joshua said, and Landyn held the tape measure down with his sneaker while they tried a four-meter run. Violette offered to collaborate on the graph, since her lines were straighter, and they split the work: she drew, he calculated, Landyn heckled.

The older skater rolled up and watched them chalk lines and chase tennis balls. "This is the weirdest use of a skate park I've seen," he said.

"It's an economy of effort," Violette told him. "One park, two assignments. We're just borrowing the concrete."

By noon Joshua had five points on his graph and a line that climbed in tidy steps. He held it up against the sky, and the line looked like the ramp on the far side of the bowl, tilted and rising.

"Same shape," he said. "The graph is a ramp."

Landyn squinted at the paper, then at the bowl. "Okay, that's actually kind of great."

"Race you to the top of it," Joshua said, and tucked the clipboard under his arm.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Silverpine smelled like pine sap and old carpet, because the staff had spent last spring trying to renovate the boathouse instead and run out of money before they got to this building. Katherine sat in front of a screen that still showed a blinking cursor, and she had exactly two days to finish her project for the Friday demo.

Her program was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime. She had the asking part working. The deciding part kept printing "prime" for everything, even 10, which was obviously wrong, though she couldn't see why, because the problem was hiding somewhere inside the loop.

"Mine works," said Marek, leaning back in his chair. "Want to test it? Give me a number."

"Nine," said Anis from across the table, not even looking up. "Bet you it says nine is prime."

"It won't," Marek said.

It did. The screen read: 9 is prime.

"That's wrong," Anis said, spinning her chair around. "Nine is three times three. It has a divisor that isn't 1 or itself."

"That's the whole rule though," Marek said. "A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself. Nine has three as a divisor, so it's out."

"Then your program's broken," Anis said.

While they argued, Katherine pulled a sticky note toward her and started testing her own idea. If a number was prime, then dividing it by every whole number between 2 and itself should never give a remainder of zero. That was the rule upside down: no divisors except 1 and itself meant no clean divisions in between. She typed a loop that tried 2, then 3, then 4, all the way up, and printed "not prime" the moment a division came out even. Then she ran it on 9.

9 is not prime.

She ran it on 7. Prime. On 9 again. Not prime. On 25, just to be safe. Not prime. Her stomach did a small flip, the good kind.

When they left the lab, the lake was choppy from the afternoon wind, whitecaps skitting across the turbulent water, and the swim docks had been roped off. Ms. Greco was stapling a notice to the corkboard by the mess hall, and she waved them over. The note read: "Demo moved to Thursday, 4 p.m., mess hall. Judges: camp director and the coding sponsors. No extensions, sorry! Bring working code. Ms. G."

Marek read it twice and went pale. "That's tomorrow. My program still thinks nine is prime."

"Show me your loop," Katherine said.

They sat on the steps of the mess hall while the wind rattled the ropes against the flagpole. Marek opened his laptop, and Katherine looked at his code. His loop checked whether the number divided evenly by 2 only, and if it didn't, he called it prime. Nine wasn't even, so nine got called prime. She didn't say any of that out loud. She just pointed at his screen.

"Try every number between 2 and your number, not just 2," she said. "Print not prime the second one divides evenly. That's what mine does."

Marek typed, deleted, typed again, and hit run. He entered 9.

9 is not prime.

He entered 17, then 21, then 49, grinning wider each time. Anis leaned over the railing above them and shouted down, "Try ninety-one, that one's tricky!" and Marek's fingers were already moving.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
Mrs. Shevchenko's note was taped to the fridge in blue ink, and Kayla read it twice while baby Theo gummed his fist in her arms. "Formula is in the cupboard. He naps around seven. Sleep rules are on the crib." Then a second line, smaller: "Text me any question, truly any question, do not guess."

Kayla had wanted this job for weeks. Liliana had told her babysitting was the fastest way to earn money for the class trip, and Kameron had laughed and said Kayla would panic the second the baby cried, which had made Kayla more determined than ever. So far, so good: Theo had eaten, burped, and only yelled a little during the diaper change, which Kayla considered a vigorous protest rather than a real complaint.

At seven, his eyelids drooped while she rocked him. She carried him to the nursery and laid him down, then spotted the blanket folded on the shelf, cream-colored and soft as a cloud. It seemed wrong to leave a baby in a bare crib on a cool evening. She reached for it.

Then she saw the card taped to the railing. It was a letter in the same blue ink: "No pillows, no blankets, no toys in the crib. Firm flat mattress only, always on his back until his first birthday. This keeps the risk of SIDS low. I know it looks strange. Please trust me." Kayla's hand stopped in the air. Theo was under one year; that part she knew for certain. Back, firm, flat, empty crib. She had almost guessed the opposite of every rule on the card.

She stood there arguing with herself. The blanket was so fluffy, and the card so blunt. But her own urge to be cozy wasn't a concept she could test on Theo. Mrs. Shevchenko had written "do not guess," and a guess was exactly what the blanket would have been. Kayla put it back on the shelf and made sure Theo was settled on his back, nothing around him but the tight-fitted sheet.

She texted a photo of the empty crib to Mrs. Shevchenko anyway, just to be sure. The reply came fast: "Perfect. Thank you." Kayla smiled, then felt a small pang: Mrs. Shevchenko would never know how close she had come to draping that blanket over him. She had done the right thing, but only barely, and the near-miss would stay her own secret. Somehow that made the success feel thinner, like earning a medal for a race you'd almost skipped.

Theo's chest rose and fell in the dim room. Kayla pulled the door almost shut and sat in the hallway with the monitor, listening to the small steady crackle of him breathing.

"Okay," she whispered to the empty hall. "I'm a babysitter now."

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, verbs used with thou usually end in -est, so "thou knowest" means "you know".
story:
Mr. Swampy passed out the photocopied pages like they were treasure maps, which Jaxson doubted, since the words on his looked like someone had spilled alphabet soup across the page. "Romeo and Juliet, Act Two, Scene Two," Mr. Swampy said. "Your job by Friday: paraphrase the speeches into modern English. Your own words."

At lunch, Jaxson slid his page across the table to Ajay. "Help. What is 'wherefore' even doing there? Why does every single word have letters stuck on the end?" He pointed at a line halfway down. "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun." That part he could handle. Then Romeo kept going, and the page turned into "thou art" and "dost" and a sentence that ended with "knowest the sound of art."

"Maybe it's a code," Ajay said, chewing. "Like a cipher."

Harlyn sat down across from them, grabbed the page, and squinted. "You know how in science we tracked those birds that migrate south, and we couldn't see the route, we had to figure it out from the data?" She tapped the margin. "Look at your data. Thou appears, and then the verbs grow tails. Knowest. Art. Dost." She slid the page back. "Count them yourself. I'm not doing your homework."

Jaxson counted. Every time the line started with thou or thee or thy, the verb that followed ended in -est or -st, or turned into art. When the line used you, the tails vanished. He flipped the page over and wrote a test sentence in his notebook: "Thou knowest the answer." Then underneath it: "You know the answer." It worked. It worked again with "thou art" meaning "you are." The rule held every single time he checked, like a handrail in the dark. He sat back, and Ajay leaned over to look at the notebook like it was a winning lottery ticket.

He was so absorbed that he didn't notice the bell, and the three of them had to pivot from the table and jog down the hall before the door swung shut. In class the next morning, Mr. Swampy called on him first to read, and Jaxson took a breath and read the stumbling line out loud, then gave the modern version without pausing. "You know how art works," he said. "Or at least you know what the sound of it is." Mr. Swampy smiled and marked something in his book. When Jaxson got his page back at the end of class, a green note in the margin read, "Resilient work. Try the whole speech tonight."

He walked home reading the speech as he went, mouthing thou knowest and hearing you know, the way you hear a friend's voice through a wall once you know who it belongs to.
